To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the IL‐1 receptor type I (IL‐1RI) is a target for LPS in the mouse brain and that this effect is mediated by the IL‐1 system; and (ii) the IL‐ 1RI gene is defective in NZB mice.
Interleukins (ILs) are cytokines produced by immune cells and are involved in the regulation of the immune system.
Interleukine‐1 receptors in the brain of autoimmune mice have a defect in their ability to bind ligand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of IL‐1 receptors in the central nervous system (CNS) in normal and autoimmune mice.

the study of the regulation of IL‐1 receptor expression in the brain, in normal and autoimmune mice, and with the study of IL‐1‐mediated effects on the stress axis, the immune response, and autoimmunity.
the study of the regulation and function of the IL‐1 system in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL‐1R type 1 in NZB mice is not functioning.
IL‐1 receptors are not expressed in the dentate of NZB mice.
IL‐ 1 receptors in brain are regulated by endogenous IL‐1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IL‐1 system is a powerful regulator for immune functions and stress responses.
IL‐1 receptors in the hippocampal dentate gyrus of autoimmune mice have a defect in their expression.
the IL‐1 system in the brain, which is involved in the regulation of the stress and immune responses, is abnormal in NZB mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IL‐1R system is involved in the regulation of the immune response.
the IL‐1R defect in NZB mice may contribute to their autoimmune disease.
the IL‐1 receptor defect is tissue‐specific in the brain of autoimmune mice.
